topics.label: Introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture within the cancer course and introduces its learning objectives.

topics.label: Genetic origins and clonal evolution of cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how mutations give rise to evolving cancer clones within the constraints of inherited susceptibility and a permissive cellular environment.

topics.label: Environmental cancer risks and interpretation of the evidence
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how evidence about environmental exposures informs our understanding of cancer risk rather than attributing cancer simply to chance or genetics.

topics.label: Infectious agents in cancer development
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections contribute to carcinogenesis, with Burkitt lymphoma providing a detailed example of interacting infectious causes.

topics.label: Environmental carcinogens and mechanisms of DNA damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental carcinogens produce DNA damage, showing how their activity depends on chemical processing and the site of exposure.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics establish why mutational initiation may require a separate growth-promoting environment for tumours to develop.

topics.label: Developmental and tissue susceptibility, with a synthesis of carcinogenic mechanisms
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics complete the account of context-dependent carcinogenesis by explaining developmental susceptibility and consolidating the preceding mechanisms of carcinogen action.

topics.label: Methods for investigating carcinogenicity and their limitations
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how researchers obtain and interpret evidence that an exposure can cause cancer, emphasizing the limits of the available methods.

topics.label: Closing summary and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This closing draws together the lecture’s conclusions about environmental cancer risks and the difficulty of assessing them for everyday risk–benefit decisions.
